proxy_language: Kanuri (Kanem-Bornu court language; Saharan family), supplemented for the Sefuwa-era court titles by Old Kanembu and Arabic loanwords
proxy_rationale: 'Gainemrìg' is not a recognizable ethnonym or toponym in the literature; the string strongly resembles 'Kanem' + 'mai' (Kanuri 'ruler') and the Sahelian later-court setting of Kanem-Bornu (c. 11th-19th c.), whose court language was Kanuri (Kanembu is the closest relative). Kanuri is well documented (Lukas, Cyffer, Hutchison, Jarrett), so it is the most defensible attested proxy for a Sahelian later court. The link between the game culture and this language is an assumption, hence low confidence. Alternatives (Hausa for Hausa city-states, Songhay/Zarma for Gao-Songhai, Mande for Mali) would be equally plausible for other Sahelian courts.
phonology: Kanuri consonants: p b t d c j k g (stops/affricates, c=[tʃ], j=[dʒ]), f s z sh (ʃ), h, m n ny (ɲ), ng (ŋ), l r (trill/flap), w y, plus a lateral fricative-like l and implosive/ejective-like reflexes in Kanembu; /p/ is marginal and often from loans, /f/ is often a reflex of p in older forms. Vowels: a e i o u plus central ə (written ə or â in older sources); vowel length is contrastive (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu) in scholarly orthography. Tone: Kanuri has a limited tone system (high/low, mostly on verbs and some nouns), not marked in standard orthography. Stress is not phonemic.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes are (C)V(C) with V(V); most native words are CV, CVC, CVCV, CVCCV. Word-initial single consonants only, no initial clusters in native words. Medial clusters are common but typically homorganic nasal+stop (nd, mb, ng, nj) or liquid+C (rg, lg, rd). Native nouns frequently end in vowels or in n, r, l, m, ng; word-final voiced stops are rare. Vowel harmony is not a strong feature. Arabic loans (via Islam, 11th c. on) add clusters and consonants such as q, kh, gh, sh, ʕ that are typically nativized (q to k, kh to h or k).
orthography: Use the standard Latin Kanuri orthography (Nigerian, Cyffer/Hutchison style): a b c d e ə f g h i j k l m n ny ng o p r s sh t u w y z, with 'c' for [tʃ], 'sh' for [ʃ], 'ny' for [ɲ], 'ng' for [ŋ]; long vowels doubled; ə written as ə or ɔ-free ascii 'e'/'a' fallback. Capitalize proper names. Arabic court titles transliterated simply (e.g. 'mai', 'galadima', 'kachella' in older English spellings; modern 'kacella').
morphology: Agglutinative, SOV language. Nouns are uninflected for gender; plural is formed by suffix -wa (e.g. a collective/plural marker on some nouns) or by suppletive/irregular forms; case marking is by postposed enclitics on the noun phrase (genitive -ben, dative/locative -ga, ablative -ndo, instrumental -do, etc.; specifics vary by dialect and source). Verbs carry person/tense/aspect/derivational prefixes and suffixes; the verb root in -a/-u/-i forms is used as agent or nominal base via suffixing -ma (agent nominalizer 'one who does') or -ye. Reduplication occurs for intensity or plurality in adjectives and some nouns. Derivational: -ma/-ya forms abstracts and agents; -rama gives instruments; -bu 'owner of' / 'having'.
compounding: Compounds and genitive phrases are head-final: modifier precedes head. 'X of Y' is Y + genitive marker + X (possessor-possessed) or simple juxtaposition of Y X with the head at the right: e.g. 'house of the king' = mai ben fato roughly 'king's house'. Titles are placed before personal names. Agent nouns 'Y-maker' are built Y + verb root + -ma (e.g. 'iron-worker' = iron + work + ma). Place names often combine a descriptive noun with a locative or an Arabic-derived baptism of the settlement ('X-ri' / 'X-ya' endings are rare; more often a bare noun phrase such as 'Birni Ngazargamu' = 'town Ngazargamu').
noun_phrase_order: Head-final: demonstratives and possessors precede the noun; adjectives follow the noun (N-Adj) in Kanuri, with numerals following as well; relative clauses precede the head. Genitive phrase = possessor + ben + possessed. Postpositions rather than prepositions.

attested_roots.gloss: sleep/lie (verbal root, mostly forming nouns by derivation)

notes: The name 'Gainemrìg' does not match any known Sahelian ethnonym; the grave accent and the sequence 'gr' are non-Kanuri, so treat it as a game-internal label and do not derive names from its spelling. Kanuri has more tonal and phonological detail than the simple orthography shows; the proxy is deliberately simplified for name-building. Titles like mai, galadima and fugəma are historically linked to the Sefuwa court of Kanem-Bornu. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word since Kanuri is not Goidelic; check names against Gaelic lexica to avoid accidental matches.
